Here’s how I’d approach it: --- ### **First, acknowledge your feelings are valid** - It’s completely normal to feel torn. You’re not "wrong" for wanting to protect someone or for feeling that silence is harmful. - **Why this is hard:** - **Family loyalty vs. moral duty:** Many cultures (including Indian families, where " family first" is often deeply ingrained) prioritize harmony and secrecy to avoid shame or conflict. AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **NTA (Not the Asshole)** *(0 in AITA scoring system)* ### Here's why: 1️ **Your feelings are valid and reasonable** - You’re not asking them to *change their lives* (e.g., "move out of Honors dorms"). You’re simply asking for basic inclusion in a group *you* chose to be part of. - Being the only person excluded from shared experiences (classes, dorms, inside jokes) *because of a structural barrier* (Honors College) is isolating. It’s not " overreacting"— it’s human. - Your shyness amplifies this pain: when a group is your only social lifeline, being consistently left out feels like a rejection of *you*, not just your academic path. 2️ **Their response was dismissive and un empathetic** - When you expressed hurt, one friend said, "You have no right to make us feel bad for being happy." **This is the problem.** - It’s not about " making them feel bad"— it’s about *acknowledging your pain*. A caring friend would say: " I didn realize this was affecting you. How can we include you more?" - Telling someone their feelings are "wrong" for being hurt is emotionally invalidating. *That* is the asshole behavior here—not your decision to step back. 3️ **You’re not being unreasonable** - **" I deserve friends who try to include me" is a healthy boundary.** - You’ve already tried talking to them. They didn’t adjust their behavior. - The Honors dorm situation isn’t their * fault* ( it’s a university policy), but * their* choice to prioritize their own convenience over your feelings * is* the issue. - **Key distinction:** - *Unreasonable:* " You *must* all move out of Honors dorms to include me." - *Reasonable:* " I feel excluded when we only hang out in Honors spaces. Can we sometimes meet at the library or a neutral spot?" You’re asking for the *latter*— not the former. ### What *could* help (if you want to try): - **" I’m not asking you to change your dorms. I just need us to intentionally plan time together outside Honors spaces. Can we try that?"** - If they still refuse or dismiss you: **It’s time to find new friends.** - You don’t " have to start over"— you can quietly build new connections while still being in this group (e.g., join clubs, study groups outside Honors). - **This isn’t " giving up"— it’s self-p preservation.** A true friend group wouldn’t make you feel like an outsider * by design*. ### Why this isn’t AITA: - **You’re not the one being unfair.** - **You’re not demanding the impossible.** - **You’re not lashing out or shaming them.** - **You’re simply choosing to protect your mental health when your friends showed zero empathy.** **Final verdict:** **NTA (0)**. The real " asshole" here is the friend who told you you have " no right" to feel hurt. *Your* feelings matter. Your well-being matters. **You deserve better.** 💛 > *Note: AITA judgments aren about " right or wrong" in a moral absolute sense—they’re about whether* **your actions** *were unreasonably harmful to others. In this case, they weren’t.* > *If you’re struggling, talk to a campus counselor. They exist to help students navigate exactly this kind of isolation.*
